# Abstract

When parents fall into two groups (for example lines and testers, or two heterotic groups) and each parent of one
group is crossed with each parent of the other, `PartialDiallel()` gives the combining ability of each group and the
specific combining ability of the crosses.

# The data

```{r data}
head(PartialDiallelData)
with(data = PartialDiallelData, expr = table(Cross1, Cross2))[1:3, ]
```

Ten parents (1 to 10) are crossed with four parents (11 to 14), in four replicates.

# The analysis

```{r analysis}
p <-
  PartialDiallel(
      y      = y
    , Rep    = Rep
    , Cross1 = Cross1
    , Cross2 = Cross2
    , data   = PartialDiallelData
    )
knitr::kable(x = p$ANOVA, digits = 4)
knitr::kable(x = p$Genetic.Components, digits = 4)
```

With $L$ and $M$ parents in the two groups, $\sigma^2_{g^I} = (MS_{g^I} - MS_s)/(BM)$,
$\sigma^2_{g^{II}} = (MS_{g^{II}} - MS_s)/(BL)$ and $\sigma^2_s = (MS_s - MS_E)/B$. `Percent` is each source's
share of the treatment sum of squares.

# Effects

```{r effects}
round(x = p$General, digits = 3)
plot(p)
```

```{r sca, fig.height = 5}
plot(p, which = "sca")
```

# Summary

Both groups show significant general combining ability; the specific combining ability of the crosses is small.

# References

Kempthorne, O. and Curnow, R. N. (1961). The partial diallel cross. *Biometrics*, 17(2), 229--250.

Kempthorne, O. (1957). *An Introduction to Genetic Statistics*. John Wiley and Sons, New York.

Singh, R. K. and Chaudhary, B. D. (2004). *Biometrical Methods in Quantitative Genetic Analysis*. Kalyani Publishers,
New Delhi.
